Normal bowel movements = 3/day to 1 every 3 days; normal stools are isosmotic

Diarrhea: abnormal frequency and liquidity of fecal evacuations; occurs when the water balance in the GI tract is disturbed

  • > 3 bowel movements/day, stool weight > 200 g/day
  • Acute diarrhea < 4 weeks – usually infectious
  • Chronic diarrhea > 4 weeks – usually non-infectious

blocks.html:
Diarrhea workup
  • Hx: nature of diarrhea (acute/chronic, bloody/non-bloody, frequency, steatorrhea), fecal urgency, incontinence, abdominal

pain, fever, weight loss, energy level, risk factors (medications/ABX, foreign travel, sick contacts, dietary Hx/water source,

ethnicity), extraintestinal manifestations of IBD (mouth ulcers, perianal disease, skin rash, eye symptoms, arthritis)

  • PEx: vital signs (fever, dehydration), weight, nutritional status, abdominal exam
  • Ix: CBC, electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, ESR, CRP, lipid profile, glucose, pancreatic enzymes, albumin, blood cultures, AXR,

microbiology (stool culture + sensitivity, stool ova + parasites, C. difficile toxin), 𝛼-1 antitrypsin, TTG, sigmoidoscopy

  • Consider hospital admission in: presence of severe systemic signs, inability to maintain hydration with oral intake, infants,

elderly, immunocompromised host

Malabsorption: inadequate absorption of nutrients from the GI tract – small bowel especially important

rows: Chronic pancreatitis (kills acinar cells), cystic fibrosis, pancreatic neoplasms, pancreatic surgery
Bacterial overgrowth in proximal small bowel
Surgery, celiac disease, Chron disease, lymphoma

blocks.html:
Drugs associated with diarrhea: acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, alcohol, ABX, antidiabetics, cholinergic agonists, dopamine

antagonists, histamine H2-receptor antagonists, immunosuppressants, levo-thyroxine, laxatives, orlistat (lipase inhibitor), potassium

supplements, prostaglandins, SSRIs, sulfasalazine

Non-inflammatory infectious diarrheas – enterotoxin-mediated alterations in fluid/electrolyte absorption/secretion; small intestine

  • Vibrio cholerae serotypes 01 and 0139 (gram-negative rod): cholera toxin activates adenylate cyclase (ATP → cAMP), ↑ Cl–

secretion, ↓ Na+ absorption, water follows NaCl in small bowel lumen; rice water diarrhea

Tx: oral/IV rehydration, ABX (doxycycline, azithromycin, ciprofloxacin), prevention (sanitation, Dukoral vaccine)

  • Food poisoning: Escherichia coli 0157:H7 (verotoxin), S. aureus, Bacillus cereus
  • Watery diarrhea: norovirus, rotavirus, giardia lamblia, cryptosporidium, cyclospora, cystoisospora belli

Inflammatory infectious diarrheas – cytotoxin-mediated destruction/invasion of mucosal cells; large intestine

  • Abdominal cramping, fever, bloody stools – NEVER give antidiarrheal agents (prolongs exposure → toxic megacolon)
  • Bacterial bloody diarrhea (CC-E-YSS): Clostridium difficile, Campylobacter jejuni (poultry), Escherichia coli 0157:H7, Yersinia

enterocolitica, Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi (Typhoid fever), Shigella dysenteriae; Vibrio vulnificus

  • Parasitic bloody diarrhea: Entamoeba histolytica, giardia lamblia

Pediatric diarrhea = excessive daily stool; liquid volume > 10 mL stool/kg body weight/day

  • Acute diarrhea < 2 weeks
  • Chronic diarrhea > 2 weeks
  • Red flags: chronicity, presence of blood/mucus/undigested food, minimal to no weight gain/weight loss, nighttime stooling,

output >> intake, no response to a discontinuation of intake

  • Celiac disease: abdominal pain/distension, loose non-bloody stools, iron-deficiency, poor growth; test IgA + TTG IgA
  • Milk protein intolerance: mucous in stool ± blood, regurgitation, healthy otherwise; dairy-free diet, hydrolyzed protein formula
  • Assess hydration status in any acute diarrheal illness – oral rehydration is the most important Tx
  • Check stool culture before starting ABX for acute diarrheal illness

blocks.html:
ROME IV criteria – functional constipation
  • Must include 2 or more of the following:

a)Straining during more than 25% of defecations

b)Lumpy or hard stools (Bristol stool form scale 1 or 2) more than 25% of defecations

c)Sensation of incomplete evacuation more than 25% of defecations

d)Sensation of anorectal obstruction/blockage more than 25% of defecations

e)Manual maneuvers to facilitate more than 25% of defecations (digital evacuation,

support of the pelvic floor)

  • f) Fewer than 3 spontaneous bowel movements per week
  • Loose stools are rarely present without the use of laxatives
  • Insufficient criteria for IBS
  • Criteria fulfilled for the last 3 months with symptom onset at least 6 months prior to Dx

Constipation workup
  • Hx: symptoms of constipation, dietary Hx (fibre/water intake), adequate time for toileting, willingness to use public bathrooms,
  • PMHx (look for 2° causes), medications, allergies, social Hx (ADLs, IADLs, abuse)
  • PEx: DRE, inspect for anal fissures/hemorrhoids/soiling, assess anal tone at rest and with squeeze, palpate for rectal mass,

exclude fecal impaction

  • Ix: CBC, calcium, TSH, colonoscopy (indicated for red flags)

Choosing Wisely: avoid performing a colonoscopy for constipation in those under the age of 50 years without family

  • o history of colon cancer or alarm features
  • Colon transit study: ingestion of 24 radio-opaque sitz markers on day 1; AXR on day 5
  • Anorectal manometry and balloon expulsion test: specialized pressure sensing catheter and inflatable balloon inserted into the

rectum to measure rectal sensation, anal pressure, anorectal inhibitory reflex, and ability to expel balloon

  • Defecating proctogram: barium instilled into rectum then defecation on a special commode under x-rays allows for the

visualization of anatomic abnormalities

  • Tx: patient education, dietary/lifestyle (adequate fluid intake, 20-30 g/day of fibre, physical activity), osmotic laxatives (17 g

PEG3350 dissolved in 8 oz water; 15-30 cc lactulose; magnesium-based), stimulant laxatives (1 tab senna, 5 mg bisacodyl), stool

softeners (100 mg docusate b.i.d., 15 mL mineral oil NOT recommended), enemas (sodium phosphate, tap water, soap suds),

secretagogues (linaclotide – 145 mcg for constipation, 290 mcg for IBS-C; prucalopride), surgery (subtotal colectomy and

ileorectal anastomosis, repair of rectocele), biofeedback (relaxation/coordination retraining of the pelvic floor)

Long-term use of laxatives will NOT lead to dependency and a “lazy colon”

  • o PEG 3350 has no electrolytes and is tasteless; PegLyte is used for bowel preparation before colonoscopy
  • o Choosing Wisely: do NOT use stool softeners alone to prevent opioid-induced constipation

  • Red flags for organic causes of constipation: onset age < 1 month, delayed passage of meconium > 48 hrs, failure to thrive,

abdominal distension, hematochezia, systemic symptoms (fever, vomiting), no response to Tx

Cirrhosis (chronic liver damage): the irreversible scarring of the liver that occurs after years of chronic insult

  • Cell death → progressive fibrosis → regenerative nodule formation; liver is shrunken, firm, and nodular

thrombocytopenia, portal hypertension

  • Dx: biopsy (gold standard), AST and ALT may be elevated or normal (hepatocytes “burn out”), ultrasound
  • Tx: liver transplantation
Ascites: the accumulation of fluid in the abdominal cavity
  • The most common complication in patients with cirrhosis; 60% of patients develop ascites within 10 years of cirrhosis Dx
  • PEx: shifting dullness, fluid wave

Dubin-Johnson syndrome: autosomal recessive condition caused by impaired intrahepatic bilirubin excretion
• Absence of the canalicular protein multidrug-resistant protein 2 (MRP-2)
• Functionally normal, enlarged, black (dark) liver; asymptomatic, chronic/recurrent jaundice
• Dx: ↑ serum direct bilirubin, normal CBC, normal liver enzymes, grossly black liver on biopsy

Rotor syndrome: autosomal recessive condition caused by impaired hepatic storage of conjugated bilirubin, which leaks out
• Phenotypically similar to Dubin-Johnson syndrome, but milder presentation; normal (regular) liver

Alagille syndrome: autosomal dominant condition caused by too few bile ducts to drain the bile, which leads to bile build-up in the liver

• Prominent forehead, triangular face, butterfly vertebrae, posterior embryotoxon, tetralogy of Fallot, pulmonary stenosis

blocks.html: GI Tip of the Day

rows:
The 2 most common causes of a patient presenting with dysphagia and a documented history of weight loss are esophageal cancer and achalasia.
Other causes of dysphagia, such as peptic stricture, are much less likely to result in significant weight loss unless very severe.

An EGD with esophageal biopsies needs to be considered in a patient with intermittent solid-food dysphagia to rule out eosinophilic esophagitis
(EoE) even in the presence of normal endoscopic findings. Eosinophil counts > 15 per hpf in the mid or proximal esophagus is extremely suggestive
of EoE and can be treated with PPI, swallowed topical steroids & esophageal dilation.

The tip for today pertains to GI history taking. For any GI and liver-related illness, always ask about NSAIDs. It is also important to always take a
detailed social history including smoking, alcohol, marijuana, and other recreational drug use. Don’t forget to elucidate any family history of GI
related malignancy, IBD, celiac or liver disease. Finally, asking about any previous endoscopic evaluations can help to determine the need for
further endoscopic investigation.

Typical symptoms of GERD (i.e. heartburn & regurgitation) are the most likely to respond to treatment with Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs). Other
symptoms potentially associated with GERD include: cough, shortness of breath, hoarseness of voice and dental enamel erosion. These so called
“extra esophageal” symptoms of GERD are less likely to respond to PPIs, mainly because they are less likely to be actually caused by GERD. If in
doubt whether the symptoms are related to GERD or not, a 24 hour pH study can be helpful.

Cyclical attacks of nausea and vomiting, known as Cannabis Hyperemesis Syndrome (CHS), have been reported with the long-term use of
marijuana; It is generally associated with heavy users of THC (i.e. Daily use for months to years) and patients often report compulsive bathing in hot
water as this may relieve their symptoms. The only effective treatment is Cannabis cessation.

Weight loss is not a typical symptom of IBS, so in a patient presenting with possible IBS and weight loss other causes need to be excluded. For
treatment of IBS always remember dietary interventions (i.e. low FODMAPs diet), psychosocial interventions and tailor medical therapy based on
predominant symptom complex.

Always consider whether a digital rectal exam is necessary when examining a patient with GI symptoms. This simple exam is often overlooked and
can be quite useful and even lifesaving if pathology such as a rectal mass is found. This should always be performed in a patient presenting with
rectal bleeding. Ensure patients are informed about what you are going to be doing, obtain consent and drape patient appropriately. Remember to
always have a chaperone present. There are very few contraindications to rectal exam: febrile neutropenia, no anus, no finger!

If suspicious for celiac disease, one can screen by ordering TTG antibodies. Always remember to order an IgA level anytime you order TTG
antibodies, because TTG can be falsely negative if IgA is low. If TTG antibodies are positive, one should always go on to confirm the diagnosis with
endoscopy and duodenal biopsies. Iron-deficiency anemia is the most common extraintestinal manifestation of celiac disease.

When working up iron deficiency anemia, don’t forget to treat the iron deficiency while investigations are pending!! Do not use serum iron to
diagnose iron deficiency anemia… use ferritin or transferrin saturation instead as they are a more reliable indicator of actual iron stores.

Remember melena is more typical of an Upper GI bleed but occasionally can be a manifestation of a proximal Lower GI bleed. Similarly, bright red
blood per rectum, is usually a manifestation of a lower GI bleed, but one always needs to be alert to the possibility that it represents a brisk Upper
GI bleed, which would be suggested if the patient is hemodynamically unstable. The most important management principal for GI bleeds is to
always resuscitate the patient aggressively first, then consider scoping them!

All patients with chronic liver disease, with or without cirrhosis, should be vaccinated for Hep A and Hep B, unless they have active infection or are
serologically immune. If a patient with compensated liver disease were to acquire an active infection with either Hepatitis A or Hepatitis B, this can
lead to severe decompensation and this can be prevented through vaccination.

Early liver cirrhosis can be present with a normal appearing liver on imaging in addition to normal liver enzymes and synthetic liver bloodwork.
High clinical suspicion is necessary. Unexplained splenomegaly, dilated portal vein, and thrombocytopenia can be early clues to the presence of
cirrhosis.

Statins are safe to use in patients with cirrhosis. Liver enzymes should be routinely monitored, and these medications can be continued as long as
liver enzymes do not elevate more than 2 times from baseline after starting statins.

Patients with acute pancreatitis needs fluids – lots of it. Ringer’s lactate is generally preferred, and patients often require 4-5L of fluid to make up
for their fluid deficit. They also require pain control and reintroduction of nutrition as soon as they are able to tolerate it (i.e. symptoms improving).
Typically they should be progressed from clear fluids to full fluids to diet as tolerated. If symptoms recur with reintroduction of food, then you may
have to back off temporarily and if prolonged NPO is expected or required may need to consider supplemental nutrition with NJ tube or rarely TPN.

In patients with hepatic encephalopathy ammonia does not correlate with the degree of encephalopathy and should not be used in the diagnosis,
rather the clinical assessment is key in making the diagnosis.

Pancreatic pseudocyst: a collection of pancreatic juice encased by a wall of fibrous or granulation tissue that occurs in or around the

pancreas as a consequence of pancreatitis or ductal leakage; > 4 weeks for form; no epithelial lining

Abdominal pain, vomiting, jaundice, recurrent pancreatitis

  • Complications: infection, hemorrhage, rupture
  • Tx: conservative if asymptomatic; drain if symptoms/complications (endoscopic, percutaneous, surgical)
  • Ductal adenocarcinomas, neuroendocrine tumours, and solid pseudopapillary neoplasms may become cystic
  • Serous cystic neoplasms: F > M, body or tail, almost always benign, DDx = metastatic renal cell carcinoma
  • Mucinous cystic neoplasm: F, body or tail, larger cysts, mucinous cells underlying ovarian stroma, may become malignant
  • Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm: M > F, head of pancreas, ducts are dilated by papillary structures lined by mucinous

cells, may become malignant

Other Pathologies

Mallory-Weiss syndrome: longitudinal lacerations at the gastroesophageal junction due to severe vomiting (alcohol use disorder,

bulimia nervosa); painful hematemesis

Zollinger-Ellison syndrome: associated with multiple peptic ulcerations in the stomach and duodenum due to excess gastrin

secretion by gastrinoma, leading to excess gastric acid production; associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) type

Gastroparesis: objectively delayed gastric emptying in the absence of a mechanical obstruction

  • Nausea, vomiting, early satiety, bloating, upper abdominal pain, weight loss
  • Etiology: Type 1 diabetics (longstanding disease, poor sugar control), idiopathic (1/3 of patients), post-viral (norovirus,

rotavirus), medications (opioids, TCAs, CCBs, dopamine agonists, anticholinergics), post-surgical, neurologic disease (MS,

Parkinson’s), autoimmune (scleroderma), hypothyroidism

  • Ix: esophagogastroduodenoscopy, CT enterography/small bowel follow through
